records.rationale: The nav rail's own background is deliberately a tad darker than --ds-surface-canvas so the sidebar reads as its own surface instead of blending flush into the workspace canvas. No generated semantic role expresses 'canvas, mixed slightly toward black' in every theme (--ds-surface-panel-subdued is already used for .item's own row-hover state; reusing it for the rail's resting background would make hover indistinguishable from rest). color-mix with a literal black is the only reliable way to guarantee darker-than-canvas across every approved theme face.
records.reviewCondition: a semantic --ds-surface-rail (or equivalent 'sidebar, distinct from canvas') role is added to the generated token set

records.rationale: overflow-y:auto makes the <nav> itself a focusable scroll container in Chromium (independent of any child .item's own focus state); suppressing its own default focus ring is intentional -- keyboard focus is always visible on whichever .item actually has it, via that item's own left-border-accent treatment (.item:focus-visible below), never a full rectangle around the entire rail. Set to the literal '0' (rather than 'none', used by .item:focus-visible's own identical-intent exception) purely so the checker's exception mechanism -- which can only resolve a match to exactly one diagnostic per rule+path -- can tell the two apart; both compute identically in every browser.
records.reviewCondition: the rail's own scroll-container focus-ring suppression is replaced by a non-focusable scroll wrapper

records.rationale: A boxed outline reads as a foreign element in this rail -- every other active/focus treatment here (.itemActive) is a left-border accent, never a full rectangle, and a boxed outline on the topmost item visually collided with GlobalFrame's border above it. Focus stays visible via the identical left-border-color change .itemActive already uses (border-left-color: var(--ds-border-selected) on the same rule), so this is a substitute focus indicator, not a removed one.
records.reviewCondition: the rail adopts a shared focus-visible primitive treatment instead of its own left-border convention

records.rationale: The group-disclosure control (chevron + uppercase category label, aria-expanded/aria-controls, collapses/expands a nav section) has no counterpart in any shared primitive: Button/IconButton are for standalone text or icon-only actions, and ListRow's closest-shaped API renders aria-pressed (list-selection semantics), not a disclosure toggle. Extracted to its own file (Desk's FaderLearnHitArea.tsx precedent) so CommandRail.tsx's own raw <button> (the nav item, a separate registered exception below) is the only one the checker finds there -- two raw <button> elements in one file always produce byte-identical DS005 diagnostic values, which the exception mechanism cannot resolve individually. D-05's 'Feature CSS Modules may own feature layout and exceptional domain visualization' carve-out -- there is no disclosure-toggle primitive in this codebase to reuse.
records.reviewCondition: a shared disclosure-toggle primitive is added to the design system

records.rationale: Each nav destination button carries aria-current="page" navigation-landmark semantics (WAI-ARIA's convention for persistent primary navigation), which the closest-shaped shared primitive (ListRow) does not support -- it renders aria-pressed (list-selection semantics) instead, and switching would both regress the existing aria-current contract CommandRail.test.tsx already asserts and weaken the nav's accessibility semantics. D-05's 'exceptional domain visualization' carve-out -- there is no aria-current-aware nav-item primitive in this codebase to reuse.
records.reviewCondition: a shared nav-item primitive with aria-current support is added to the design system
